cues.text: Section one: Governance, and why organisations need it.
Imagine a bank whose developers can independently purchase cloud services, grant database access and deploy software, all without approval or monitoring.
The teams may be technically competent, yet the organisation cannot reliably control its spending, its security or its legal obligations.
Governance solves exactly this problem: the problem of direction and accountability.
So let us define it.
IT governance is the system of decision rights, structures, policies and oversight that ensures technology supports organisational objectives, delivers value and manages risk.
It helps to separate governance from management.
Management plans and executes activities within the direction that governance sets.
Put simply, governance asks whether the right things are being done, while management asks how to do them effectively.
Now consider the five central concerns of governance.
They are strategic alignment, value delivery, risk management, resource management and performance measurement.
Keep these five in mind, because they frame most governance decisions.
Governance also depends on clear roles.
A governing board sets risk appetite and strategic direction.
Executives translate that direction into priorities.
Managers implement policies.
Auditors independently assess whether the controls are working.
And one point deserves emphasis: accountability cannot simply be outsourced to a vendor.
An organisation may hand work to a supplier, but it remains answerable for the outcome.
Finally, governance is expressed through four kinds of documents, and it is important to tell them apart.
A policy states a requirement.
A standard specifies mandatory criteria.
A procedure describes how to perform a task.
A guideline recommends an approach.
Here is one example that connects all four.
A policy requires the protection of customer information.
A standard then requires encryption.
A procedure explains key rotation.
And a guideline recommends secure implementation patterns.
Notice how the layers move from the general requirement, to the mandatory criteria, to the step-by-step task, and finally to recommended practice.
